newsitem.title: LAOS: Decades-old bombs plague most of Laos - study.
newsitem.headline: Decades-old bombs plague most of Laos - study.

text.p: Decades-old bombs remain scattered over nearly every province of Laos and claim about 200 victims a year, a new study has found.

The first comprehensive survey of unexploded ordnance, known as UXO, revealed that 11,000 Laotians have died or been wounded by bombs and bomblets since 1973, Ian Mansfield, adviser to the National UXO Programme, or Lao UXO, said on Friday.
"Over the last 10 years, someone has been injured or killed about every second day from a bomb dropped more than 20 years ago," he told Reuters in an interview.
The survey, due to be released next week, represents the best picture yet of the UXO problem in Laos, he said.

Between 1964 and 1973, Laos suffered protracted ground battles and some of the heaviest aerial bombardment in history as the United States tried to cut off North Vietnam's access to the Ho Chi Minh trail, which runs along eastern Laos.
During that period, the Americans launched over 500,000 bombing missions, or the equivalent of one plane load of bombs every eight minutes around the clock for nine full years.

Many bombs never exploded and killed years later when detonated by an unsuspecting child or farmer. After the war, UXO injured or killed over 1,000 people annually, though that rate has since dropped to 200 a year, the survey found.
About half of all incidents are deadly, the survey said.
Particularly troublesome are bomblets, or "bombies", said Charles Kraus, coordinator of the U.S. Humanitarian Demining Office in Vientiane.
About 670 bomblets, which range in size from a golfball to a softball and spray ball bearings up to 30 metres (yards), were released from every cluster bomb dropped over Laos, he said.
As many as 30 percent never exploded, according to Lao UXO.

The year-long survey, conducted by Lao UXO and Handicap International, covered 8,000 of 11,000 villages in Laos and found that bombies were responsible for half of all casualities, Mansfield said, with many children mistaking them for toy balls.
Bombies and other UXO were found in 16 of Laos' 18 provinces and administrative districts, with heaviest concentrations in the north and along the Ho Chi Minh trail, Mansfield said.

To combat the problem, Lao UXO, with help from the United Nations, United States, Germany, Handicap International and other donors, are conducting community awareness programmes, clearance programmes and medical training, Mansfield said.
